reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the creator actively encourages viewers to place Bitcoin into BitConnect lending by presenting daily interest, capital release, and earnings from participation as a way to make money and change their lives. The creator also promotes an affiliate link and explicitly encourages viewers to refer others for multi-level commissions, making the video an investment solicitation rather than a neutral demonstration.

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's position by what he says he knows. He admits losing money in earlier experiments that turned out to be Ponzi schemes, calls himself new to this, and treats withdrawal as an unanswered question. His stated purpose is to put in a small test amount and see whether returns can actually be taken out. That is a materially different message from claiming the investment is proven to pay: the promised follow-up depends on a result he has not yet observed.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to a daily rate, referral commissions and an affiliate link, but those do not erase the speaker's explicit doubt about getting paid back. Even his explanation of the bot is qualified with "as far as I understand." The quoted rate is a description of the platform's terms, not testimony that a withdrawal has succeeded or a guarantee to viewers. The link is promotional, but promotion alone does not turn this first test into a claim of verified returns.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Uncertainty does not make the video chiefly a warning. The speaker moves from his own test to inviting viewers to join him, advises them to start small, and says he will put a link in every video because they want to make money. The cited doubts qualify his confidence, but do not undo that invitation or the lending pitch.

opening.argument: The video is structured as a first-use walkthrough. The speaker explains how he deposited Bitcoin, waited for confirmation and exchanged it into the platform wallet; then he narrates the lending step while calling the recording a chronicle of his experience. He asks viewers to teach him more and says he will show a withdrawal only when he can make one. The investment screen is the subject of the demonstration, not independent evidence that its displayed terms will be fulfilled.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening correctly identifies the lending terms and the referral invitation, but it treats those portions as the whole video. The speaker also spends time explaining the deposit and exchange sequence and openly says he has not established whether money can come back out. Showing the lending interface and explaining its terms are consistent with documenting a process; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate that the speaker has verified a return.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can also solicit participation. Here the speaker does more than explain controls: he tells viewers they can make money by referring others, urges interested viewers to try it with him, and directs them to his affiliate link. The tutorial framing does not account for those calls to participate in the lending and referral program.

opening.argument: The referral discussion describes a disclosed affiliate program, with specific commission tiers, rather than concealing that the speaker has an incentive to share a link. The lending interface also discloses a capital-release period, while the speaker says he has yet to test whether he can withdraw returns. Those facts leave important claims unproved: neither a successful payout nor a guaranteed one follows from the displayed terms. The link deserves scrutiny, but its presence alone does not establish that the speaker is hiding the program's conditions.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening infers a deceptive solicitation from the rates and multi-level commissions. But the speaker identifies the referral percentages instead of disguising them, and the lending confirmation visibly states that capital remains locked for 299 days. The evidence establishes an investment and an affiliate incentive; it does not establish that the speaker promised immediate access to capital or represented his untested withdrawal as already successful.

citations.quote: Anyway, so it's 5%, 3%, and 2%.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Disclosure of commissions and a lockup does not make this an ordinary referral offer. The speaker asks viewers to lend money for daily interest, celebrates the prospect of substantially higher earnings, and invites others to join through his affiliate link. The missing proof of a payout limits what can be concluded about outcomes, but not what the video is promoting.
